articles.body: Shadow AI discovery is the part of AI governance that IT teams inherit without being asked. Nobody sends a memo announcing that the sales team pasted a customer contract into a chat tool, that an engineer connected a coding assistant to the production repository, or that finance trials four summarisation tools on last quarter's board pack. The usage simply exists, and the first question leadership asks is one nobody can answer from existing dashboards: how much of this is happening, and what data has left the building? The comfortable answer, that the company has a policy and a list of approved tools, describes intent rather than reality. Discovery is a separate discipline with its own data sources, its own blind spots, and its own false positives.

articles.title: Is It Safe to Delete ~/Library/Caches on a Mac? How to Clear Cache Safely
articles.excerpt: Yes—most subfolders inside ~/Library/Caches are safe to delete on a Mac, as long as you quit running apps first, remove only the contents inside (never the Caches folder itself), and skip Apple system…
articles.body: Yes—most subfolders inside ~/Library/Caches are safe to delete on a Mac, as long as you quit running apps first, remove only the contents inside (never the Caches folder itself), and skip Apple system caches and sensitive tool data. Apps automatically recreate their cache files the next time you open them, so the only normal side effect is a slightly slower first launch or re-downloading cached assets. What you should not touch are macOS's system-wide /Library/Caches and /System/Library/Caches folders—macOS manages those itself. Also keep expectations realistic: clearing cache reclaims disk space, not RAM or CPU performance; in fact, rebuilding caches can briefly use a little extra disk and network activity right after cleanup.

articles.title: How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work
articles.excerpt: How realistic are the zero-g sports we see in sci-fi? We talk to Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, to find out.
articles.body: Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing after launching into suborbital space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit.

articles.title: Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance
articles.excerpt: These strange geological features may offer clues to the Red Planet's watery past.
articles.body: NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface. While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years. In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

articles.title: 'Avengers: Doomsday' gets final trailer, explaining why Steve Rogers is back and showing an epic battle with the X-Men
articles.excerpt: Marvel Studios’ first Avengers film since 2019 is less than a month away, and it might be the big-screen team-up event we thought impossible only ten years ago.
articles.body: The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday just landed, and it finally puts the spotlight on our boy Steve Rogers. Avengers: Doomsday has been promising the scale and excitement the MCU has often been lacking since the Infinity Saga. Previous trailers played it safe, mostly setting up the conflict and introducing Victor Von Doom. Now it’s time for one last explosive look at the film before it tries to conquer cinemas next month. Disney and Marvel Studios have just released a "final trailer" that puts the focus back on Steve Rogers — no longer Captain America but still ready to use Mjolnir — and Thor as the veterans leading the New Avengers, former colleagues, the Fantastic Four, and even Fox's X-Men (after some first-encounter fights, of course) against Doom and his followers.

articles.title: The remains of a long-dead volcano on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 23, 2026
articles.excerpt: Just imagine the ancient, Martian lava flowing.
articles.body: An image of Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, produced by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet. What is it? The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus. This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera. Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains.
